study.title: Leviticus 7 - Sacrifices, holiness and priestly provision
study.overview: Leviticus 7 gathers complementary instructions on the guilt sacrifice, the peaceful offering, and the portions for the priests. The chapter shows that worship in Israel was not only a matter of religious feeling, but of concrete holiness: blood, fat, flesh, ritual purity and consumption times were regulated before the LORD. At the same time, the text reveals that God provides sustenance to the priests through offerings, while maintaining the distinction between what is holy, what is unclean and what can be received in communion with Him.

outline.title: Offer for guilt and parts reserved for priests
outline.explanation: The first verses repeat and broaden the legislation of the guilt offering: it is "very holy thing, the blood is applied to the altar, the fat is burned to the LORD, and the flesh is eaten by the priests in holy place. Afterwards, the text includes instructions on the burnt offering and the offer of cereals, highlighting that certain parts belong to the priests as a provision linked to worship.

outline.title: Peaceful offer, thanksgiving and purity requirement
outline.explanation: The peaceful offer appears in its forms of thanksgiving, voting and voluntary offer. The chapter regulates the time when the meat can be eaten and prohibits it from being consumed in an unclean state or after the due deadline. Impurity makes the meal incompatible with the sanctity of the offering and bears guilt for those who profane it.

outline.title: Prohibition of fat and blood; priestly portion; conclusion of the chapter
outline.explanation: The LORD forbids the consumption of fat and blood throughout Israel, linking these realities to the sacrifice that belongs to God. It is then specified that the breast moved and the elevated thigh of the peaceful offerings are left for Aaron and his children. The chapter closes by summarizing all the deals dealt with and situating these instructions on Mount Sinai in the Sinai Desert.

study.context: The chapter is presented as instruction given by the LORD to Moses for the children of Israel, associated with Mount Sinai and the wilderness of Sinai. This indicates that the norms belong to the period of Israel's formation as a covenanted and organized people to worship God in a holy way. The text also shows a liturgical structure in which sacrifices support worship and, at the same time, the subsistence of priests.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter emphasizes that God is holy and establishes concrete means by which sinners can approach him. The guilt offering and the sin offering are treated as realities of reconciliation, linked to blood and the burning of fat, showing substitution and consecration. The peaceful offering, especially in thanksgiving, reveals that communion with God includes gratitude, communion and obedience to its conditions. The prohibition of eating blood and fat points out that life belongs to the LORD and that not everything that is attached to sacrifice can be appropriate by man. Finally, the portion of the priests shows that worship also orders community life, because God cares for those who serve in the sanctuary through the offerings of the people.

scholarViews.insight: The peaceful offering could be presented as an expression of gratitude; in this case, it was accompanied by an offer of cereal with cakes, obles or pies prepared with olive oil, and also lighted breads.
Peaceful offerings could be given in thanksgiving for special mercies received, or in fulfillment of a vow made in time of distress; thus, the offerer's intention was central to this sacrifice.
The animals found dead were considered unclean because they did not have the blood drained; therefore, their fat could not be offered to the LORD or food, although it could serve for other uses.

questions: What does the text teach about the difference between approaching God with gratitude and doing it in a ritual way, but without obedience?
How does the prohibition of eating blood and fat help to understand that life belongs to the LORD?
How does the provision of priestly portions correct a vision in which spiritual ministry is separated from the material responsibility of the community?
study.practice: This chapter calls the believer to treat worship with real reverence, not as an empty routine. In practice, this means to thank God sincerely, to offer him the best, to respect what he declares holy and sustain, responsibly, those who dedicate themselves to spiritual service. It also leads us to examine whether we are trying to enjoy the benefits of communion with God without submitting to the conditions established.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not define here, in detail, the technical difference between each type of sacrifice beyond what the text itself informs; therefore, any broader distinction depends on other passages of Leviticus. It is also not possible to affirm, only with these notes, dates or additional historical circumstances beyond the general reference to Mount Sinai and the Sinai Desert.
